Your first tax and pension letters, decoded
articles.previewMarkdown:
Most newcomers to Tokyo lose their first month to a loop: the bank wants a phone number, the phone carrier wants a bank account, and both want proof of an address you registered at a ward office whose website is only half translated.

The good news is that the loop has a known exit. Errands in Japan are a **chain**, and once you do them in the right order, each one unlocks the next.

## Start at the ward office, not the bank

Within 14 days of moving into your home, you must register your address at the local ward office (*kuyakusho*). This single visit produces the document everything else depends on: your address written on the back of your residence card.

Bring:

- Your residence card and passport
- Your rental contract or the exact address in Japanese
- A pen and about two hours of patience

While you are there, ask to enroll in National Health Insurance at the same counter. It saves a second trip.

articles.title: Writing Business Email to Japanese Companies
articles.subtitle: Templates and the unwritten rules for getting replies from Japanese partners.
tableOfContents: Why your cold email was ignored
The five-part structure Japanese readers expect
Subject lines that survive a shared inbox
articles.previewMarkdown:
A well-written English email can still fail in Japan. Not because of grammar, but because of **structure**: Japanese business readers expect information in a particular order, and an email that skips steps feels abrupt or risky to forward to a manager.

## The decision is rarely made by the person you email

Your contact will usually need to explain your proposal to someone else. Every email you write should be easy to forward with one line added on top. That means:

1. Say who you are and how you found them in the first two lines.
2. State one clear request, not three.
3. Put dates, numbers and attachments where they can be copied without editing.

The full guide walks through each part with examples, then gives you templates for first contact, follow-ups, quotes and polite refusals.

articles.previewMarkdown:
Kyoto has more than 1,600 temples, and almost every visitor sees the same ten — at the same time of day.

This guide is built around one simple idea: **timing beats location**. The famous sights are beautiful at 7 a.m. and exhausting at 11 a.m. The plan below moves you against the crowd, so you reach each place just before or just after the tour buses.

## Before you go

- Buy a rechargeable IC card on arrival; buses and most shops accept it.
- Keep cash for small temples and family-run restaurants.
- Book one special dinner in advance and leave the rest to chance.
